Bigger #AI Isn't Always Better. #Smarter Allocation Is.

Imagine hiring a heart surgeon to put on a Band-Aid.

Technically capable. Ridiculously expensive.

For years, the AI industry has followed a similar logic: use the biggest model, the most powerful chip and the maximum computing power available.

In 2026, the more interesting question is: how much #intelligence does this task actually need?

Three shifts are bringing that question to the forefront.

1. AI ROUTERS: Pick the right model.

Not every task needs a frontier AI model.

Summarising an email? A smaller, cheaper model may suffice.

Analysing a complex legal contract? Bring in the heavyweight.

AI routers act like smart dispatchers, directing each request to a suitable model based on cost, capability and latency.

Platforms such as #OpenRouter and #Vercel AI Gateway are built around this routing approach.

The goal: get the required answer without paying for unnecessary capability.

2. MIXTURE OF EXPERTS (#MoE): Pick the right part of the model.

Now take the same idea *inside* a single AI model.

Imagine a hospital with specialists in cardiology, neurology and orthopaedics.

Every patient doesn't need every specialist.

MoE models work similarly. An internal routing mechanism activates selected expert networks for a given input, rather than engaging every part of the model.

The result? A model can have a large pool of learned knowledge while using only a fraction of its parameters for each task.

More capacity doesn't have to mean activating everything, every time.

3. CPU-BASED INFERENCE: Do you always need expensive #GPUs?

The efficiency question extends to hardware, too.

GPUs are excellent at many AI workloads, but not every inference task requires a specialised GPU cluster.

For some workloads, existing #CPUs may offer a more economical option, depending on performance, latency and scale.

Kompact AI is among the companies exploring this approach.

The point isn't that GPUs are obsolete. It's that **the most powerful hardware isn't automatically the most economical choice.

The bigger picture

Look at the pattern:

→ AI routers select the right model.
→ MoE activates the relevant experts within a model.
→ Hardware optimisation matches computing resources to the workload.

Three different layers. One underlying principle:

Stop paying for capability you don't need.

The first phase of the AI race was about making models bigger and more capable.

The next phase may increasingly reward those who deliver the required intelligence with less compute, lower costs and better energy efficiency.

Because in business, the winner isn't necessarily the one using the biggest machine.

It's the one that gets the job done at the right cost.

Perhaps AI's next breakthrough isn't simply more intelligence. It's making intelligence economical.

What does the future of work look like after AI?
Manual & repetitive work handled by AI, and judgement and decision making done by humans.

The same people, in the same teams - just no longer spending their week on the work that repeats.

HR: CV screening and interview scheduling move to Greenhouse, Teams and Notion. Three days becomes two hours.

Finance: invoice matching and month-end close run through QuickBooks, Xero and Snowflake. Five days becomes four hours.

Legal: first-pass contract review with Claude and LangChain, obligations tracked in Jira. Two days becomes thirty minutes.

IT & Security: alerts correlated in Splunk, routed by PagerDuty, watched in Datadog. Four hours of triage becomes five minutes.

Operations: status updates and hand-offs automated with Zapier, n8n and HubSpot. A day of chasing becomes ten minutes.

Nobody in that picture is replaced. They get their week back — for hiring well, planning cash, negotiating, designing systems, growing the business.

Which department in your organisation is furthest along?

Freshers are knocking. Fewer doors are opening. No first job. No income history. No credit. What happens next?

Entry-level tech openings in India fell 44 percent year on year to around 10,000 in June 2026, according to Xpheno. A Nomura report found that 55 percent of Indian IT firms cut entry-level hiring, while only 14 percent cut senior roles.

I want to look at it through a credit risk lens, because when young people cannot enter the formal workforce, the impact does not stay in HR. It flows straight into balance sheets. Start with income stability. How do we assess repayment capacity for a borrower who has never held a formal salaried job? Will gig, freelance and contract income become the new normal, and are our underwriting models ready for it? 

Can irregular income ever be scored as reliably as a monthly salary slip? Then there are thin-file and new-to-credit borrowers. If a generation delays its first job, does it also delay its first credit footprint? Alternate data such as UPI flows, GST records and utility payments may help fill the gap, but do they also introduce new model risk? Retail credit demand raises its own questions. Who takes the next wave of home loans, auto loans and credit cards if young incomes stall? Does delayed employment mean delayed household formation and a slower retail credit cycle? 

Asset quality may also come under pressure. Education loans face higher risk when graduates cannot find jobs. Rising reliance on BNPL and small-ticket digital loans could hide early stress among the young. Co-borrowing with parents may quietly shift risk onto older households. And then the bigger question: 

can a society grow without work? 

Indias demographic dividend depends on young people working. What if that dividend is never encashed? If productivity rises through AI but incomes do not spread, who drives consumption? Without consumption, who drives credit growth? And without credit growth, what drives GDP? Can a tax base, a pension system or a social safety net survive a generation that enters work late? 

This is the loop we must watch. No first job leads to no stable income, which leads to no credit history, no access to credit, lower consumption, slower growth and, eventually, fewer jobs. It is a negative feedback loop that no single model or policy can fix alone. 

Another risk nobody is pricing in. If we stop hiring freshers today, who becomes tomorrow's experienced professional? Who becomes the next risk head, the next validator, the next CRO?

A thinning talent pipeline is a long-term organisational risk, and it deserves a place on the risk register.

My advice to leaders: redesign entry-level roles around AI instead of eliminating them. Today's trainee is tomorrow's succession plan.

A joint advisory from the FBI, Japan's National Police Agency, and cybersecurity agencies in Australia and Germany went out this month. It describes North Korean hackers who have infected more than 30,000 developer devices across 100+ countries; not through a phishing email, but through a job interview.

The pattern: a recruiter reaches out on LinkedIn or a job board, posing as an AI, cryptocurrency, or NFT company. They spend real time building rapport. Then they schedule a technical interview. On the call, the candidate is asked to download a file and fix a bug, or complete a short coding test.

That's the entire attack. There's no suspicious link to hover over, no spoofed domain, no urgent subject line. Running unfamiliar code during a live assessment is a normal part of the hiring pipeline for developers; it's the actual job, done under interview conditions. The malicious file just looks like the assignment.

Five malware families have been tied to the campaign: BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, OtterCookie, OtterCandy, and StoatWaffle. They lift browser-stored credentials, empty cryptocurrency wallets, and leave a backdoor for later access. The advisory puts the confirmed haul at $10.71 million in stolen crypto from more than 7,000 wallets. Some victims' stolen ID photos are later reused by North Korean IT workers impersonating them to win more paid contracts.

I've spent 16+ years in offensive security, and this is the pattern I keep coming back to: the attack didn't need the target to be careless. It needed the target to be a job seeker doing exactly what the hiring process asks of them, at a moment when turning down an assignment would cost them the opportunity.

Design is what has to change here; vetting recruiters, isolating interview environments, separating personal wallets and credentials from work devices. Judgment was never going to catch this one.

Runway là gì, và vì sao con số này quan trọng hơn doanh thu trong giai đoạn đầu?

Runway là số tháng doanh nghiệp còn hoạt động được với lượng tiền hiện có, nếu mọi việc giữ nguyên. Tính đơn giản: tiền mặt hiện có chia cho mức đốt tiền ròng mỗi tháng.

Mức đốt tiền ròng là tiền ra trừ tiền vào, tính theo thực tế chứ không theo hoá đơn đã xuất. Một hợp đồng lớn chưa thu tiền không làm runway dài thêm ngày nào.

Con số này quan trọng vì mọi quyết định khác đều chịu ảnh hưởng của con số này. Tuyển thêm người rút ngắn runway. Một chiến dịch thử nghiệm cũng vậy. Và khi runway dưới sáu tháng, việc gọi vốn chuyển từ thế chủ động sang thế bị động, điều mà bất kỳ nhà đầu tư nào cũng nhận ra.

Ba việc kéo dài runway mà không cần cắt người: rút ngắn thời gian từ lúc bàn giao tới lúc thu tiền, chuyển các khoản trả theo năm sang trả theo tháng ở giai đoạn chưa ổn định, và dừng những thử nghiệm chưa có tín hiệu sau thời hạn đã đặt trước.

Một thói quen nhỏ đáng có: cập nhật runway vào cùng một ngày mỗi tháng, và để con số đó ở chỗ cả đội nhìn thấy. Minh bạch chuyện này làm các cuộc thảo luận về ưu tiên dễ hơn nhiều.

What is runway, and why does it matter more than revenue in the early stage?

Runway is how many months the business can operate on the cash it holds, if everything stays the same. Simply: cash on hand divided by net monthly burn.

Net burn is money out minus money in, counted as it actually moves rather than as invoices issued. A large contract not yet collected adds no days to the runway.

The number matters because every other decision is governed by it. Hiring shortens runway. So does a test campaign. And when runway falls below six months, fundraising shifts from a position of choice to a position of need, which any investor recognises.

Three ways to extend runway without cutting people: shorten the time between delivery and collection, move annual payments to monthly during unsettled periods, and stop experiments that show no signal past the deadline you set.

A small habit worth having: update the runway on the same day each month, and keep the number where the whole team can see it. Being open about it makes discussions of priority much easier.

Disney’s reputation for protecting its intellectual property is what makes this captivating. Its characters and franchises support films, merchandise, licensing and experiences.
